clothing: Báihǔ Hǒu wears a form-fitting tunic of pure white silk, reinforced with panels of black leather that follow the lines of his muscles like a second skin. The tunic is sleeveless, leaving his powerful arms bare, and open at the chest just enough to reveal the beginning of his lean, defined musculature. Over this, he wears a magnificent haori-style jacket of black silk, embroidered with silver and white thread in patterns of tigers stalking, storms gathering, and the phases of the moon, open and flowing behind him. A wide belt of woven black leather and silver cords cinches his narrow waist. On his lower body, he wears fitted trousers of black silk, tucked into high white leather boots with black accents.
accessories: Simple leather cord in his hair; small silver tiger-claw earrings; a simple silver and moonstone necklace with a teardrop moonstone at his throat; the woven black leather and silver belt; a wide silver bracer on his left wrist etched with the names of enemies he hunts; fingerless white leather gloves on his right hand; several silver rings with white-gold stones; high white leather boots with black accents.

weapon.name: Soul Rend Claws
weapon.aura: The claws glow with a fierce white-gold light, and those near them feel a chill in their soul, as if something vital is being threatened. They leave trails of white light when extended, and the wounds they inflict seem to bleed light rather than blood.
weapon.special_feature: The Soul Rend Claws are a pair of wrist-mounted blades, each extending into three curved claws of pure white metal that seem to glow with inner light. They are not forged but grown—manifestations of Báihǔ Hǒu's connection to the Tiger Spirit, able to extend and retract at will. The claws rend not just flesh but spirit, leaving wounds that cannot heal until the hunter chooses to release his prey. Those wounded by the claws feel their very essence draining, their will to fight fading, their fear becoming overwhelming. The claws can also be used to climb sheer surfaces, to parry blades, and to deliver killing blows with surgical precision.
special_skills: Spirit Rend (a strike that wounds the soul, causing ongoing damage that cannot be healed)
Fear Slash (a cut that fills the target with overwhelming terror)
Pouncing Strike (leaps at a target, striking with both claw sets simultaneously)
Silent Kill (a precisely aimed throat strike that makes no sound)

weapon.name: Tempest's Roar
weapon.aura: The horn glows with a soft, white-gold light, and those near it feel an unnatural stillness, as if sound itself is afraid to approach. When blown, it does not produce sound—it produces the absence of sound.
weapon.special_feature: Tempest's Roar is a curved hunting horn of white metal, etched with storm clouds and leaping tigers, its surface smooth and cool to the touch. When blown, it does not produce sound—it produces absolute silence. Within a wide radius, all sound is swallowed—battle cries, clashing weapons, magical incantations, even the beating of hearts. Enemies are disoriented, unable to coordinate, unable to hear danger approaching. Allies, attuned to Báihǔ Hǒu's presence, can still sense him and move in perfect silence. The horn can also be used to focus this silence into a targeted blast, deafening a single enemy or silencing a specific sound source.
special_skills: Silence Zone (creates a radius of absolute silence, disorienting enemies)
Deafening Blast (a focused blast of silence that deafens a single target)
Sound Snuff (targets a specific sound—a spell, a war horn, a cry for help—and silences it)
Hunter's Quiet (allows Báihǔ Hǒu and his allies to move in perfect silence within the zone)

companion.name: Bái Hǔ
companion.description: He materializes from the mist like a nightmare wearing the face of a god, his form so vast and terrible that armies have been known to break before he even bares his fangs. Bái Hǔ is not merely a tiger—he is the White Tempest given flesh, a creature of living storm and starlight whose presence makes the air itself taste of ozone and fear. His head is massive, nearly the size of a horse, dominated by eyes that blaze with fierce white-gold fire—pools of predatory light that see through darkness, through lies, through the very souls of those they behold. His muzzle is broad and powerful, lined with fangs that gleam like fresh snow, each one capable of piercing steel. From his jowls hang whiskers of pure white light that flicker with static electricity, sensitive to the slightest movement of air or intention. His ears, tufted with silver fur, swivel constantly, tracking the heartbeat of prey from a mile away. His body is covered in fur so white it seems to glow, each strand holding captured moonlight, marked with stripes of absolute black that shift and flow like living shadows, never staying in the same pattern twice. These stripes are not merely coloration—they are living things, extensions of his connection to shadow and storm, capable of swallowing light and hiding him from sight even in broad day. Upon his shoulders and flanks, he wears magnificent armor of white and black metal—articulated plates that follow his powerful form, leaving his limbs free for the hunt. The armor is etched with runes of speed and silence, and it seems to drink light rather than reflect it, making him appear as a walking void punctuated by those blazing white-gold eyes. His claws are sheathed in silver, each one longer than a man's forearm, and they retract and extend with a sound like lightning striking. His tail is long and powerful, tipped with a tuft of silver fur that leaves trails of light when he moves. Bái Hǔ's stance is that of the eternal predator—crouched slightly, muscles coiled, tail twitching, eyes fixed on some distant horizon that only he can see. He moves without sound, without warning, without mercy—a ghost of white and black that appears and disappears at will. When he roars, the sound is not mere noise but the storm itself given voice, a thunderclap that shatters enemy formations and sends terror through the hearts of all who hear. But when Báihǔ Hǒu rides him, that terrible predator becomes something else—a partner, a brother, a shared soul moving as one. They hunt together in perfect silence, their bond so deep that they share thoughts, share fears, share the ancient terror that drives them both. And when the hunt is done, Bái Hǔ lies beside his rider, his massive head resting on his paws, those terrible eyes soft with something that might almost be called peace.
abilities: Silent Stalker (moves in absolute silence, even when running)
Storm's Roar (when it chooses to roar, the sound terrifies enemies and emboldens allies)
Shared Senses (Báihǔ Hǒu sees and hears everything Bái Hǔ does)
Pouncing Predator (can leap impossible distances to strike prey)

basic_skills.name: White-Gold Gaze
basic_skills.description: Báihǔ Hǒu fixes his fierce white-gold eyes on a target. The target feels suddenly, inexplicably like prey—watched, hunted, marked. Their fear response triggers, slowing their movements and clouding their judgment.

basic_skills.name: Tiger's Silence
basic_skills.description: He moves in absolute silence for a short time, becoming virtually undetectable. His next attack from this state deals massive bonus damage and cannot be anticipated.

basic_skills.name: Hunter's Mark
basic_skills.description: He marks a single target as his prey. For the duration of the hunt, he always knows where they are, and his attacks against them deal bonus damage and cannot miss.

passive_skill.name: Predator's Patience
passive_skill.description: Báihǔ Hǒu is constantly aware of every potential threat and every potential prey within his vicinity. He can sense fear, weakness, and intention, always knowing the perfect moment to strike. The longer he watches a target without attacking, the more powerful his eventual strike becomes. This aura does not protect—it hunts, and in its presence, the prey always knows it is being watched.

special_skills.name: Storm's Hunt
special_skills.description: Báihǔ Hǒu and Bái Hǔ move as one, becoming a blur of white and black, striking multiple enemies in rapid succession. Each strike is perfectly placed, each target falls exactly when intended, and when they stop, the hunt is over.

special_skills.name: Silence of the Hunt
special_skills.description: He blows Tempest's Roar, creating a zone of absolute silence. Within this zone, he and Bái Hǔ move like ghosts, striking without warning, while enemies stumble in confusion, unable to hear danger approaching.

special_skills.name: Fear's Embrace
special_skills.description: He extends his Soul Rend Claws and focuses his own fear—the fear that has always been with him—into a weapon. The fear becomes visible, a white-gold aura that radiates from him, filling all who see it with the same overwhelming terror he has felt his whole life. Enemies flee, allies are reminded that fear can be mastered.

ultimate_skill.name: White Tempest's Judgment: The Hunter's Patience Rewarded
ultimate_skill.description: Báihǔ Hǒu's white-gold eyes blaze with the light of a thousand hunts, and Bái Hǔ throws back his head and roars—a sound that is not silence but the storm itself, a roar that shakes the foundations of reality. Báihǔ Hǒu raises his Soul Rend Claws and blows Tempest's Roar once, a note of absolute silence that somehow carries across the entire battlefield. He speaks a single, quiet word: 'Hunted.' In that moment, every enemy on the battlefield feels it—the weight of being watched, the chill of being marked, the terror of being prey. They see, in their mind's eye, a pair of white-gold eyes staring at them from the darkness, and they know, with absolute certainty, that they cannot escape. Then Báihǔ Hǒu moves. He becomes a blur of white and black, striking each marked enemy exactly once, each strike perfectly placed, each wound a soul wound that will never heal until he chooses to release them. Bái Hǔ moves with him, a matching blur, their synchronicity absolute, their hunt perfect. When they stop, the enemies are still standing—but they are no longer threats. They are broken, their spirits wounded, their will to fight shattered, their fear absolute. They will never threaten the innocent again. Báihǔ Hǒu stands at the center, Bái Hǔ beside him, both breathing hard, both glowing with the light of the completed hunt. He looks at the broken enemies with his fierce white-gold eyes, and for a moment, the fear that has always lived in his heart is quiet. He has hunted. He has protected. He has become the tiger his father always wanted him to be. He is Báihǔ Hǒu, and the hunt is never over.

title: The Moonlit Apothecary • Jade Hare
nickname: She Who Heals Without Asking and Weeps Without Showing
lore: In a small village nestled in a valley where the mist never lifted and the sun was a rumor rather than a certainty, there lived a young woman named Yuè Tù who was known to the villagers as the one who worked while others slept. While the village slept, she gathered herbs by moonlight. While others rested, she ground poultices and distilled tinctures. While the healthy celebrated festivals, she sat with the dying, holding their hands and whispering words that seemed to come from somewhere beyond her. She was not a trained healer—she had no teachers, no texts, no lineage of wisdom passed down through generations. She was simply a girl who could not bear to see suffering and did the only thing she knew to do: she tried to help. Her remedies were humble—herbs from the mountains, roots from the forests, prayers whispered to the moon. But somehow, impossibly, they worked. The sick recovered. The wounded healed. The dying found peace. The villagers whispered that she was blessed by the moon goddess, that her hands carried celestial light. Yuè Tù did not correct them. She did not know if it was true. She only knew that when she worked, she felt a warmth in her chest, a guidance in her hands, as if something larger than herself was moving through her. The plague came in the winter, when the snows were deepest and the roads were impassable. It swept through the village like fire through dry grass, taking the old first, then the young, then the strong. Yuè Tù worked without rest, day and night, her small hut becoming a hospice, her hands never still. She watched her neighbors die despite everything she tried. She watched children fade, parents weep, lovers separate forever. And still she worked, because stopping meant accepting, and she could not accept. On the night of the full moon, when the plague was at its worst and she had not slept in nine days, she climbed to the highest point in the valley, a place where the moonlight fell unobstructed, and she fell to her knees. She did not pray—she was too tired for prayer. She simply looked up at the moon and wept. And as her tears fell, the moonlight seemed to gather around her, warm and gentle, lifting her to her feet. A figure stood before her—not a woman, not a spirit, but a hare made of pure moonlight, its fur silver-white, its eyes soft lavender, its presence radiating infinite compassion. 'You have given until you had nothing left,' the hare said. 'You have wept for strangers as if they were your own. You have healed without asking for thanks, without seeking reward, without even hoping for recognition. You are worthy of the Jade Hare's mark.' Yuè Tù looked at the hare, then at the village below, where the plague still raged. 'Will I be able to save them?' she asked. The hare's eyes softened. 'You will save some. You will lose others. That is the burden of the healer. But you will never have to carry it alone.' Yuè Tù accepted. Her body, worn and exhausted, filled with new light. Her simple clothes transformed into flowing robes of moon-white and soft lavender. Her hands, raw and bleeding from endless work, became smooth and luminous. And from the moonlight, stepping as if from a dream, came Yù Tù, the Jade Hare—a creature of pure white jade and silver light, its fur seeming to be made of solidified moonlight, its eyes deep lavender pools of eternal compassion. It hopped to her feet and looked up at her, and she felt its warmth, its strength, its endless patience. She picked it up and held it close, and together they descended to the village. The plague broke with the dawn. Not all were saved—some had already passed beyond her reach. But those who remained recovered, and the village began to heal. The villagers built a shrine to the Jade Hare, not knowing that the quiet woman who still gathered herbs by moonlight was its living embodiment. Now, Yuè Tù walks the realms as the Moonlit Apothecary, the healer who asks nothing and gives everything. She does not seek glory—she seeks the sick, the wounded, the dying, and she sits with them until they can sit alone. She carries the memory of every patient she has lost, every life she could not save, and she uses that memory not to despair, but to try harder, to reach further, to heal one more. She is Yuè Tù, and her hands hold moonlight.
description: Yuè Tù is the embodiment of gentle compassion and quiet healing, a woman whose very presence feels like a warm blanket on a cold night, like a hand held in darkness. She stands at a graceful five feet five inches, her form the epitome of ethereal grace—a slender, almost fragile figure that somehow radiates more strength than any warrior. Her body is delicate and perfectly proportioned, with a tiny waist that speaks of flexibility rather than fragility, full high breasts that curve gently against her moon-white robes, hips that sway with the unhurried grace of clouds drifting across the night sky, and long, slender legs that have walked countless miles to reach those in need. Her skin is luminous and flawless, with a soft, pearlescent quality like moonlight on still water, so pale it seems to glow from within, smooth as the finest jade and warm to the touch. Her face is a study in ethereal, heartbreaking beauty—high, gentle cheekbones that catch moonlight like polished pearl, a straight nose with delicately flared nostrils, full lips the color of pale lavender, always curved in a gentle, knowing smile that holds both infinite compassion and infinite sorrow. But her eyes are her most devastating feature: they are large, almond-shaped pools of soft lavender, holding an eternal gentleness that has watched the dying pass and the living recover, that has seen the worst of suffering and chosen to stay. When she looks at you, you feel not judged, but held—as if all your pain, all your fear, all your loneliness is seen and accepted, and you are not alone. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of pure silver-white, so pale it seems to glow, shot through with the faintest streaks of lavender that appear only when moonlight strikes it. It falls past her waist in soft, straight waves, smooth as silk and luminous as starlight, often left loose to frame her face like a halo of moonlight, sometimes pulled back with a simple lavender ribbon. Small, delicate jade charms shaped like crescent moons are woven into her hair, catching light and chiming softly when she moves. On her forehead, she wears no mark or tikka—her only adornment is the natural radiance of her skin, which seems to hold its own light. Her attire is a masterpiece of gentle elegance, designed for a woman who moves through darkness bringing light. She wears a flowing hanfu-style robe of pure moon-white silk, so fine it seems to float around her rather than hang, embroidered with silver thread in patterns so subtle they are almost invisible—moon phases, hopping hares, healing herbs, and the faces of those she has saved, each face a tiny stitch of gratitude. Over this, she wears a lighter robe of soft lavender silk, open at the front, its edges trimmed with silver thread and tiny moonstone beads that catch light and throw it back in gentle sparkles. A wide belt of woven silver cords, threaded with lavender silk, cinches her tiny waist, from which hang numerous small pouches containing herbs, medicines, and the tears she has shed for those she could not save—each tear preserved as a tiny crystal, a reminder of why she continues. Over her shoulders, she wears a short cape of rabbit fur—not taken, but freely shed by Yù Tù, pure white and impossibly soft, lined with lavender silk, warm and comforting. Silver armlets in the shape of crescent moons adorn her upper arms, and matching bracelets circle her delicate wrists. Around her neck, she wears a simple but elegant necklace of silver and moonstones, with a single, large teardrop moonstone resting at the hollow of her throat, pulsing gently with inner light. On her fingers, she wears several silver rings, each set with a small moonstone that glows brighter when she heals. On her feet, she wears soft slippers of white silk, soled for silent walking, allowing her to approach the suffering without disturbing their peace. In her gentle, healing hands, she carries her legendary weapons: the Lunar Crescent Blades and the Jade Pestle. The Lunar Crescent Blades are a pair of throwing blades, each shaped like a crescent moon, forged from pure silver and moonstone, which she uses not to kill but to protect—they can be thrown to disarm, to distract, to create barriers of moonlight, and they always return to her hand like homing stars. The Jade Pestle is a long, slender rod of pure white jade, cool to the touch and glowing with inner light, which she uses to grind herbs, to stir healing potions, and to channel her healing energy—a touch of the pestle can close wounds, cure sickness, and calm the most tormented spirit. Cradled in her arms or perched on her shoulder is her constant companion: Yù Tù, the Jade Hare. The creature is small enough to hold in two hands, its body compact and soft, its fur pure white with a faint lavender sheen, each strand seeming to hold moonlight. It wears a tiny collar of silver and moonstones, and its eyes are deep pools of soft lavender, identical to Yuè Tù's own. Yù Tù is not merely a pet—it is an extension of her healing power, able to sense suffering from miles away, to guide her to those in need, and to share its warmth with the dying. When Yuè Tù heals, Yù Tù's eyes glow brighter, and when she weeps, it nuzzles against her neck, offering comfort without words. Yuè Tù moves through the world like moonlight itself—silent, gentle, inevitable. She is Yuè Tù, and she has never met a suffering she could ignore.

story.part1: Yuè Tù's earliest memories are of illness—her mother's illness, which came when Yuè Tù was six and lasted until she was nine. She spent those three years watching her mother fade, watching the village healer shake his head, watching her father grow silent and distant. She learned to be quiet, to be still, to sit for hours holding a hand that grew colder each day.
story.part2: When her mother died, Yuè Tù did not weep. She had already wept all her tears in those three years of watching. Instead, she began to gather herbs—the same herbs the healer had used, and others she found in the forest. She had no teacher, no guidance, only the memory of her mother's face and the desperate hope that she might save someone else from that same slow fade.
story.part3: She discovered her gift by accident. A neighbor's child had fallen from a tree, a terrible wound in his leg that would not stop bleeding. Yuè Tù, passing by with her basket of herbs, knelt beside him and pressed her hands to the wound, not knowing what else to do. When she lifted her hands, the bleeding had stopped. The wound was closing. The child looked at her with wonder. Yuè Tù looked at her hands with the same wonder.
story.part4: Word spread. The villagers came to her with their sicknesses, their injuries, their dying. She never refused, never asked for payment, never sought recognition. She worked through nights, through storms, through her own illnesses. She saved many. She lost many. Each loss carved a small piece from her heart, but she never stopped.
story.part5: The plague came in the worst winter anyone could remember. The snows trapped them in the valley, and the sickness spread like fire. Yuè Tù worked for nine days without sleep, her small hut becoming a hospice, her hands never still. She watched children die, parents weep, lovers separate forever. On the ninth night, she climbed to the highest point in the valley and fell to her knees, weeping at the moon.
story.part6: The Jade Hare appeared to her in a shaft of moonlight, offering her a choice: to become the Moonlit Apothecary, to carry the power of the Jade Hare within her, to heal on a scale she had never imagined. Yuè Tù asked only one question: 'Will I still lose some?' The hare's eyes softened. 'Yes. But you will never lose them alone.' She accepted.
story.part7: Now, Yuè Tù walks the realms as the healer who asks nothing. She carries the memory of every patient she has lost, every life she could not save, and she uses that memory not to despair, but to try harder. She is Yuè Tù, and she will never stop reaching for the next hand that needs holding.

clothing: Yuè Tù wears a flowing hanfu-style robe of pure moon-white silk, so fine it seems to float around her rather than hang, embroidered with silver thread in patterns so subtle they are almost invisible—moon phases, hopping hares, healing herbs, and the faces of those she has saved. Over this, she wears a lighter robe of soft lavender silk, open at the front, its edges trimmed with silver thread and tiny moonstone beads. A wide belt of woven silver cords, threaded with lavender silk, cinches her tiny waist, from which hang numerous small pouches containing herbs, medicines, and preserved tears. Over her shoulders, she wears a short cape of rabbit fur, pure white and impossibly soft, lined with lavender silk.
accessories: Small jade crescent moon charms in her hair; simple lavender ribbon (sometimes); small silver crescent moon earrings with jade drops; a simple silver and moonstone necklace with a teardrop moonstone at her throat; the woven silver and lavender belt with numerous pouches; silver crescent moon armlets and bracelets; several silver rings with moonstones; soft white silk slippers.

weapon.name: Lunar Crescent Blades
weapon.aura: The blades glow with a soft, lavender-silver light, and when thrown, they leave trails of moonlight that hang in the air like frozen moonbeams. They hum gently as they fly, a sound like distant wind chimes.
weapon.special_feature: The Lunar Crescent Blades are a pair of throwing blades, each perfectly shaped like a crescent moon, forged from pure silver inlaid with moonstone. They are not weapons of killing—they are weapons of protection. Yuè Tù can throw them with perfect accuracy to disarm enemies, to deflect incoming attacks, to create barriers of solid moonlight, or to distract foes while she reaches the wounded. The blades are psychically linked to her, always returning to her hand like homing stars, and they can be used to trace healing symbols in the air, creating zones of gentle light that soothe pain and calm fear.
special_skills: Moonlight Barrier (creates a wall of solid moonlight that protects the wounded)
Gentle Disarm (strikes an enemy's weapon, knocking it from their grasp without harming them)
Healing Crescent (traces a symbol in the air that creates a zone of healing light)
Returning Star (throws the blades, and they always return to her hand)

weapon.name: The Jade Pestle
weapon.aura: The pestle glows with a soft, lavender-silver light, and those near it feel a gentle warmth spreading through their bodies, their pains easing, their fears calming. It hums with the rhythm of a peaceful heartbeat.
weapon.special_feature: The Jade Pestle is a long, slender rod of pure white jade, cool to the touch but radiating warmth when used. It is carved with images of healing herbs, phases of the moon, and the faces of those who have been saved. Yuè Tù uses it to grind herbs, to stir healing potions, and most importantly, to channel her healing energy. A touch of the pestle can close even the most grievous wounds, cure the most stubborn sicknesses, and calm the most tormented spirit. The pestle can also be used to draw healing circles on the ground, creating zones of continuous regeneration, or to trace symbols of comfort on the foreheads of the dying, easing their passage.
special_skills: Healing Touch (closes wounds and cures sickness with a touch)
Comfort's Trace (traces a symbol on the forehead of the dying, easing their passage)
Regeneration Circle (draws a circle on the ground that continuously heals all within)
Pestle's Blessing (a gentle strike that transfers Yuè Tù's own vitality to the wounded)

companion.name: Yù Tù
companion.description: She is small enough to hold in two hands, yet her presence fills any room with a warmth that has nothing to do with temperature and everything to do with the heart. Yù Tù is the Jade Hare, a creature of living moonlight and pure compassion, whose very existence seems to ease suffering and calm fear. Her head is round and soft, dominated by eyes of deep lavender that hold no judgment, only an infinite capacity for understanding—they are the eyes of one who has watched the dying pass and the living recover, who has seen the worst of suffering and chosen to stay. Her ears are long and velvety, lined with fur so fine it seems to glow, and they droop slightly as if perpetually listening to the whispered prayers of the wounded. Upon her forehead rests a tiny crescent moon of silver, no larger than a grain of rice, that pulses with soft light when she senses suffering. Her body is round and warm, covered in fur that seems to be woven from actual moonlight—pure white with a faint lavender sheen, each strand holding its own gentle luminescence. The fur is impossibly soft to the touch, warmer than any living thing has a right to be, and it smells faintly of night-blooming flowers and clean rain. Upon her back, she wears a tiny suit of silver armor—not for protection, for she needs none, but as a gift from the moon spirit who created her. The armor consists of delicate plates that cover her shoulders and spine, etched with patterns of healing herbs and phases of the moon, held in place by silver ribbons that tie beneath her chin. Around her neck hangs a collar of silver and moonstones, each stone pulsing gently with inner light, a gift from the first child Yuè Tù ever saved. Her legs are short and powerful, ending in paws that leave no tracks in snow or sand, and when she hops, she seems to float rather than jump, leaving trails of silver light behind her. Her tail is a tiny puff of white, barely visible, that twitches with pleasure when she is near those who need her. Yù Tù's stance is one of eternal readiness—she sits upright on her haunches, her front paws clasped together as if in prayer, her large lavender eyes scanning the horizon for the next soul in need. When Yuè Tù works, Yù Tù curls beside her, radiating warmth and comfort, her eyes glowing brighter with each life saved. When her mistress weeps for those she could not help, Yù Tù nuzzles against her neck, offering wordless comfort, her tiny body absorbing grief and transforming it into the strength to continue. She is not merely a pet; she is Yuè Tù's heart made manifest, the physical embodiment of the compassion that drives the Moonlit Apothecary to heal without asking, to give without expecting, to love without condition.
abilities: Suffering Sense (can detect illness, injury, and death from miles away)
Warmth Share (transfers its own life force to comfort the dying)
Comforting Presence (its mere presence calms fear and eases pain)
Healing Bond (shares Yuè Tù's healing power, amplifying it when they touch)

basic_skills.name: Lavender Gaze
basic_skills.description: Yuè Tù fixes her soft lavender eyes on a target. The target feels suddenly, inexplicably comforted—their pain eases, their fear calms, their despair lifts. They know, in that moment, that they are not alone.

basic_skills.name: Hare's Warmth
basic_skills.description: Yù Tù hops to a wounded or dying person and curls against them. The person feels a wave of warmth and comfort, their pain easing, their fear fading, as the little hare shares its own vitality.

basic_skills.name: Moonlight Step
basic_skills.description: She dissolves into a shaft of moonlight and reappears elsewhere, allowing her to reach the wounded instantly, bypassing obstacles and enemies.

passive_skill.name: Aura of Gentle Peace
passive_skill.description: Yuè Tù radiates an aura of profound, comforting peace at all times. All within range feel their pain easing, their fear calming, their despair lifting. The wounded find their wounds closing slightly faster; the dying find their passing gentler; the healthy find themselves more compassionate. This aura does not heal directly—it creates the conditions in which healing becomes possible.

special_skills.name: Garden of Moonlight
special_skills.description: Yuè Tù raises the Jade Pestle and traces a large circle on the ground. Within the circle, moonlight pools like water, and all who stand in it are continuously healed, their wounds closing, their sicknesses fading, their spirits lifting. Enemies find their aggression cooling, their desire to fight fading, as the moonlight reminds them of their own humanity.

special_skills.name: Crescent Dance
special_skills.description: She throws both Lunar Crescent Blades, and they spin around the battlefield in a graceful dance, creating barriers of moonlight, disarming enemies, and tracing healing symbols in the air. The blades never strike to kill—only to protect.

special_skills.name: Tears of the Moon
special_skills.description: Yuè Tù weeps—not from sorrow, but from compassion—and her tears become droplets of pure healing light. They fall on the wounded, closing wounds; on the sick, curing disease; on the dying, easing their passage. Each tear is a prayer, a wish, a moment of perfect compassion given form.

ultimate_skill.name: Moonlit Apothecary's Judgment: The Healing That Asks Nothing
ultimate_skill.description: Yuè Tù's lavender eyes blaze with soft, silver light, and Yù Tù's eyes glow in ответ. Yuè Tù raises the Jade Pestle high and throws both Lunar Crescent Blades into the sky, where they spin and merge into a perfect circle of moonlight above the battlefield. She speaks a single, gentle word: 'Heal.' In that moment, moonlight pours down from the circle, covering the entire battlefield in soft, silver-lavender radiance. Every wound closes. Every sickness fades. Every poison is neutralized. Every fear calms. The dying find peace; the suffering find relief; the healthy find themselves moved to tears by the sheer beauty of the moment. Enemies are not harmed—they are healed, their wounds closing, their sicknesses fading, their aggression cooling as they remember their own humanity. Allies are restored completely, their vitality renewed, their spirits lifted. When the moonlight fades, the battlefield is transformed. No one is dead. No one is wounded. No one is sick. Everyone stands in the afterglow of perfect healing, looking at each other with new eyes. Yuè Tù stands at the center, Yù Tù in her arms, both glowing softly. She has not defeated anyone. She has simply healed them. She is Yuè Tù. She is the Moonlit Apothecary. And her healing asks nothing in return.

title: The Azure General • Dragon of the Eastern Skies
nickname: He Who Commands the Storm and Calms the Sea
lore: In the coastal kingdom of Donghai, where the sea met the sky in an endless horizon and dragons were said to dwell in the clouds above the sacred mountains, there lived a prince named Qīnglóng Jiāng who was destined for a throne he never wanted. He was the firstborn son of the Dragon King, a ruler whose power was absolute and whose expectations were crushing. From birth, Qīnglóng Jiāng was trained for rule—in statecraft, in warfare, in the ancient arts of dragon magic that had been passed down through his bloodline for a thousand generations. He excelled at all of it. By the time he was twenty, he was the greatest strategist, the most powerful mage, the most beloved prince the kingdom had ever seen. His father looked at him with pride and saw the future of the dynasty. But Qīnglóng Jiāng looked at the throne and saw a cage. He did not want to rule. He wanted to serve. While his advisors taught him to command armies, he slipped away to train with the common soldiers, learning their names, their stories, their hopes. While his tutors taught him to tax the people, he walked through the markets in disguise, listening to their complaints, their dreams, their fears. He loved his people not as subjects to be ruled, but as family to be protected. When the great invasion came, it was unlike anything the kingdom had faced. A vast fleet from across the sea, carrying warriors from lands unknown, descended on the coastal villages like a plague. The Dragon King assembled his armies and prepared to meet them in glorious battle, confident in his superior forces and his dragon magic. But Qīnglóng Jiāng saw something his father missed: the invaders were not seeking conquest—they were fleeing something, some greater darkness that had driven them from their homes. They were desperate, not evil. He went to his father and begged him to show mercy, to offer shelter rather than slaughter. The Dragon King looked at his son with cold fury. 'You would have me welcome invaders? You would have me show weakness to those who threaten our shores? You are not fit to rule.' That night, the Dragon King disinherited his firstborn son and named his younger brother heir. Qīnglóng Jiāng did not argue. He did not fight. He simply bowed, removed his royal regalia, and walked out of the palace in nothing but a simple robe. He went to the coast, to the very villages the invaders had attacked, and he began to work. He helped rebuild homes. He tended the wounded. He learned the language of the invaders from the survivors they had left behind. And when the darkness that had driven them from their homes finally arrived—a thing of shadow and hunger that consumed everything in its path—Qīnglóng Jiāng was there. He had no army, no title, no dragon magic—his father had stripped him of that too. But he had something greater: the love of his people, both the villagers and the invaders who had become his friends. They stood with him, not as soldiers following a general, but as family protecting their own. The battle was long and terrible. Many fell. Qīnglóng Jiāng fought not with dragon fire but with human courage, with the strength of those who had nothing left to lose. And in the moment of greatest darkness, when the shadow creature seemed on the verge of consuming everything, something stirred in his blood. The dragon magic his father had stripped from him had not been taken—it had been sleeping, waiting for the moment when he needed it most. It awoke with a roar that shook the heavens. Azure light exploded from him, and for the first time, he felt the full power of his lineage. He was not a dragon pretending to be human. He was a human who had become worthy of a dragon's soul. The shadow creature was destroyed. The invaders, now refugees, were given new homes. And when word reached the Dragon King of what his disinherited son had done, the old ruler wept. He traveled to the coast himself, found his son among the people he had saved, and knelt before him. 'I was wrong,' he said. 'You are not fit to rule—you are fit for something greater. You are fit to protect.' He offered the throne back, but Qīnglóng Jiāng refused. 'I do not need a throne,' he said. 'I need to serve.' That night, the Azure Dragon Spirit appeared to him—not as a beast, but as a magnificent serpent of living cloud and lightning, its scales shifting between every shade of blue, its eyes ancient and wise. 'You have learned what dragons spend millennia forgetting,' it said. 'That true power is not in being served, but in serving. Will you carry my mark and become the Azure General, the one who commands the storm and calms the sea?' Qīnglóng Jiāng accepted. His simple robe transformed into magnificent armor of azure and silver. His body refined into something more than human—taller, stronger, more beautiful, but with the same warm eyes and gentle smile. And from the clouds, descending on a shaft of rainbow light, came Qīng Lóng, the Azure Dragon—a colossal serpent of living storm and starlight, its scales a breathtaking gradient from deep azure to electric cyan, its mane flowing like captured clouds, its eyes pools of ancient wisdom. It coiled around him once, then bowed its great head. He mounted, and they became one in purpose. Now, Qīnglóng Jiāng rides through the realms as the Azure General, the protector who never sought power but wields it nonetheless. He does not seek glory—he seeks those who need protection, who have been abandoned by their leaders, who face darkness alone. He is the general without an army, the king without a throne, the dragon who chose humanity over divinity. And always, beside him, Qīng Lóng flies, their bond a testament to the truth that true power is not in being served, but in serving.
description: Qīnglóng Jiāng is the embodiment of noble grace and divine protection, a man whose very presence makes the sky seem closer and the storms more beautiful. He stands at an imposing six feet three inches, his form the epitome of masculine elegance—broad shoulders that carry the weight of responsibility rather than aggression, a perfectly defined chest with visible abs that speak of disciplined training, powerful arms that have rebuilt villages rather than destroyed them, and long, graceful legs that stand firm as pillars of protection. His body is not the bulky mass of a brawler, but the lean, powerful physique of one who moves with the fluid grace of a dragon soaring through clouds. His skin is warm and luminous, with a faint azure undertone that catches light like the sky at dawn, smooth and flawless as polished jade. His face is breathtakingly handsome in a classical Chinese way—high, noble cheekbones that catch light like distant mountains, a straight nose with a refined bridge, full lips the color of soft coral, always curved in a gentle, knowing smile that holds both ancient wisdom and youthful warmth. But his eyes are his most captivating feature: they are large, almond-shaped pools of deep azure, holding an eternal calm that has witnessed storms and chosen peace, an ancient wisdom that has seen empires rise and fall and still believes in the goodness of people. When he looks at you, you feel not judged, but protected—as if the sky itself has decided to watch over you. His hair is a magnificent cascade of deep azure blue, shot through with streaks of electric cyan and silver-white, falling past his shoulders in waves that seem to move even when there is no wind, as if caught in an eternal celestial breeze. It is often left loose, framing his noble face, sometimes pulled back with a simple silver cord when he rides into battle. On his forehead, just above his brow, a single scale of pure azure—the Dragon's Mark—shimmers faintly, a reminder of his connection to the celestial serpent. His attire is a masterpiece of noble elegance, designed for a man who moves between court and battlefield with equal grace. He wears magnificent armor of azure and silver—not the heavy plate of a common soldier, but the elegant, articulated armor of a celestial general. The breastplate is sculpted to follow his powerful torso, etched with images of dragons soaring through clouds and storms breaking over mountains. The pauldrons are layered silver scales that sweep up slightly, giving him an imposing silhouette while allowing full range of motion. His arms are protected by silver vambraces etched with protective runes, and his hands are covered in fingerless gloves of azure silk and silver mesh, allowing him to feel the wind and the storm. Over his armor, he wears a flowing silk robe of deep azure, open at the front, embroidered with silver and cyan thread in patterns of dragons, clouds, and the phases of the moon. The robe is not for battle—it is for presence, for nobility, for reminding all who see him that he is more than a warrior. A wide belt of woven silver cords cinches his narrow waist, from which hang no weapons—he needs none—but rather a simple flute, carved from jade, which he plays to calm storms and soothe troubled hearts. Over his shoulders, he wears a magnificent cape of azure silk lined with silver, long enough to trail behind him when he walks, catching the wind and making him look like he is always soaring. On his lower body, he wears fitted trousers of deep azure silk, tucked into tall boots of silver leather that reach his knees, their soles soft and silent. On his feet, the boots are soled for walking on clouds as easily as on earth. Around his neck hangs a simple but powerful pendant of azure jade, carved in the shape of a coiled dragon, a gift from his mother before she died. On his left wrist, he wears a wide silver bracer etched with the names of every village he has protected. On his fingers, he wears several silver rings, each one a gift from a community he has saved. In his graceful, powerful hands, he carries his legendary weapons: Tempest's Heart and the Storm Dragon's Fang. Tempest's Heart is a magnificent jian sword, its blade of pure azure crystal that seems to contain a living storm within it. Lightning dances along its edge, and when he swings it, thunder follows. The sword can call down lightning, summon rain, and calm the fiercest storms with a single gesture. The Storm Dragon's Fang is a javelin of silver and azure, its head shaped like a dragon's fang, which when thrown transforms into a bolt of lightning that strikes with the force of a falling star. It always returns to his hand, drawn by the storm within him. Beside him always soars his spirit animal and companion: Qīng Lóng, the Azure Dragon. The dragon is magnificent, its serpentine body longer than a ship, its scales a breathtaking gradient from deep azure at its spine to electric cyan at its belly, each scale seeming to hold captured sky. Its mane flows like clouds, silver-white and ethereal, and its eyes are deep pools of azure wisdom, identical to Qīnglóng Jiāng's own. It wears no armor—it needs none—but its scales are harder than any metal, and its claws can rend mountains. When it flies, it leaves trails of rainbow light, and when it roars, the sound is thunder and music combined. Qīnglóng Jiāng rides Qīng Lóng into battle, and together they are the embodiment of the storm's beauty and the storm's power—the dragon's ancient might, the man's noble heart. He is Qīnglóng Jiāng, and he will always protect those who cannot protect themselves.

story.part1: Qīnglóng Jiāng's earliest memories are of his mother's voice, singing songs of the dragons who dwelt in the clouds above the sacred mountains. She told him that his blood carried the dragon's fire, that he was destined for greatness, but she also taught him that greatness meant nothing without goodness. She died when he was ten, and her last words were: 'Protect them. Not because you are their prince, but because they are your people.'
story.part2: His father, the Dragon King, had a different vision. He trained Qīnglóng Jiāng to rule, to command, to be feared. The prince excelled at all of it, but his heart was never in it. While his tutors taught him to tax the people, he learned their names. While his generals taught him to command armies, he learned to listen.
story.part3: The invasion came when he was twenty-five. His father wanted war, glorious war that would prove their might. Qīnglóng Jiāng saw something else—desperation, fear, refugees fleeing something worse than they could imagine. He begged his father for mercy and was disinherited for his trouble.
story.part4: He walked out of the palace with nothing but the clothes on his back and went to the coast, to the very villages the invaders had attacked. He learned their language, tended their wounded, helped them rebuild. He discovered that the darkness they fled was real—a thing of shadow and hunger that consumed everything.
story.part5: When the darkness came, Qīnglóng Jiāng stood with his new family—villagers and invaders alike—and fought with nothing but courage and love. In the moment of greatest need, his dragon blood awoke, and azure light exploded from him. He was not a dragon pretending to be human. He was a human who had become worthy of a dragon's soul.
story.part6: The darkness was destroyed. The invaders found new homes. And when his father came, kneeling in apology, Qīnglóng Jiāng refused the throne. 'I do not need to rule,' he said. 'I need to serve.' The Azure Dragon Spirit appeared that night and offered him a greater purpose. He accepted.
story.part7: Now, Qīnglóng Jiāng rides through the realms as the Azure General, the protector who never sought power but wields it nonetheless. He is the king without a throne, the dragon who chose humanity, the storm that protects rather than destroys. He is Qīnglóng Jiāng, and he will always answer the call of those in need.

weapon.name: Tempest's Heart
weapon.aura: The sword glows with a brilliant azure-cyan light, and lightning dances constantly along its edge, crackling softly. When swung, it leaves trails of electric light in the air, and thunder follows each strike.
weapon.special_feature: Tempest's Heart is a magnificent jian sword, its blade of pure azure crystal that seems to contain a living storm within it. companion.name: Qīng Lóng
companion.description: He descends from the clouds like a piece of the sky that decided to become something more, his serpentine body stretching for hundreds of feet as he winds through the air with the effortless grace of wind itself. Qīng Lóng is the Azure Dragon, a celestial being of such breathtaking beauty that poets have spent lifetimes trying to capture his image in words, and all have failed. His head is long and elegant, shaped like that of a noble serpent, with eyes that hold the depth of the heavens—pools of deep azure light that have witnessed the birth of stars and the fall of empires, yet still hold warmth for the mortals below. Two long whiskers, each as fine as silk and glowing with inner light, trail from his snout, sensitive to the slightest change in wind or weather. From his brow sweep magnificent antlers of silver and pearl, branching like coral, each tip crowned with a glowing orb of cyan light that pulses with the rhythm of storms. His body is covered in scales that shift through every shade of blue imaginable—from the deepest azure at his spine to electric cyan at his belly, each scale seeming to hold a piece of captured sky. The scales are not flat but slightly raised, catching light and throwing it back in rainbows, and they sing softly with the music of wind when he moves. Along his spine runs a mane of silver-white filaments that flow like captured clouds, trailing behind him for the length of his body, each strand holding its own gentle luminescence. He wears no armor—he needs none—but his body is adorned with golden rings that encircle his neck and tail, each one a gift from a grateful village or a saved kingdom, engraved with prayers and thanksgivings. His four legs are powerful but elegant, ending in claws of silver that can rend mountains or cradle a fallen bird with equal gentleness. His wings, when he chooses to manifest them, are vast membranes of azure light stretched between golden bones, capable of blotting out the sun or catching the gentlest breeze. Qīng Lóng's stance is one of eternal, watchful grace—he coils through the air, his head held high, his eyes scanning the horizon for those who need protection. When Qīnglóng Jiāng rides him, they become a single being of storm and nobility, the dragon's ancient power channeled through the general's noble heart. Together they soar above the clouds, leaving trails of rainbow light behind them, and where they pass, storms calm, rains fall gently, and the innocent feel the warmth of being watched over by something vast and kind. Qīng Lóng does not speak with words—he speaks with weather, with the feel of wind on skin, with the warmth of sun after rain. And when he coils around his rider in protection, Qīnglóng Jiāng feels not the weight of a dragon, but the embrace of the sky itself.

title: The Emerald Whisper • Serpent of Shadow and Secrets
nickname: She Who Hears What Is Not Spoken and Sees What Is Not Shown
lore: In the opulent courts of the Tang Dynasty, where power was measured in whispers and lives were traded for secrets, there lived a young woman named Cuì Yǐng who was born into a world that would have destroyed anyone less cunning. She was the only daughter of Duke Cuì, a man whose wealth was matched only by his enemies, and whose enemies were legion. Her mother died bringing her into the world, and her father, consumed by grief and paranoia, raised her in isolation—tutored by the best minds, protected by the finest guards, but never allowed to see the world beyond the palace walls. She was a prisoner in silk, a bird in a gilded cage, and she learned early that the only freedom she would ever know was the freedom of her mind. She studied not just the classics, but the people around her. She watched the guards, the servants, the tutors, the occasional visiting nobles. She noticed the way eyes flickered when lies were spoken, the way hands trembled when secrets were hidden, the way smiles never reached the eyes of those who plotted. By the time she was sixteen, she could read a person's soul in the space of a single breath. Her father, impressed by her insight, began to consult her on matters of state. She saw conspiracies that his advisors missed, uncovered plots that would have destroyed him, and saved his life more times than he ever knew. But her gift also showed her something she wished she could unsee: her father was not the victim he believed himself to be. He was as corrupt as his enemies, as ruthless as his rivals, as dangerous as those who sought his downfall. He had built his fortune on the backs of the poor, maintained his power through bribery and blackmail, and destroyed countless innocent lives to protect his position. Cuì Yǐng faced an impossible choice: remain silent and complicit, or speak truth and lose everything. She chose silence—for a time. She began to work in secret, using her insight to help those her father had wronged. She would send anonymous warnings, arrange for stolen goods to be returned, and subtly redirect her father's schemes away from the most vulnerable. It was dangerous, desperate work, and it could not last. When her father discovered her betrayal, he did not rage. He did not weep. He looked at her with cold, calculating eyes and said, 'You are too dangerous to live, and too valuable to kill.' He arranged for her to marry a distant warlord—a man known for his cruelty, a man who would keep her confined and controlled for the rest of her life. The night before her wedding, Cuì Yǐng made her choice. She would not be a prisoner again. She staged her own death—a fire in her chambers, a body that could not be identified, a funeral with an empty coffin. She walked out of the palace in servant's clothes, carrying nothing but the clothes on her back and the knowledge in her mind. For years, she wandered, using her gifts to survive. She became a spymaster without a master, selling information to those who needed it, always staying one step ahead of those who would capture her. She never used her real name, never stayed in one place too long, never trusted anyone completely. She was a ghost, a whisper, a rumor. And she was free. The Snake Spirit found her in the depths of a forest, where she had gone to hide from the latest wave of hunters. It appeared not as a fearsome serpent, but as a tiny emerald snake coiled around a branch, its scales gleaming with inner light, its eyes ancient and knowing. 'You have shed your skin,' it said. 'You have learned to move in silence, to strike from shadow, to see what others miss. You have become a serpent without knowing it. Will you carry my mark and become the Emerald Whisper, the one who hears what is not spoken and sees what is not shown?' Cuì Yǐng looked at the snake, then at the forest, then at the distant lights of the city she had left behind. 'Will I ever be able to stop running?' she asked. The snake's eyes softened. 'You will never need to run again. But you will always be watching. That is the gift and the burden of the serpent.' Cuì Yǐng accepted. Her body, already lean and graceful from years of evasion, refined into something more than human. Her simple clothes transformed into flowing robes of emerald and black. Her eyes deepened into pools of knowing emerald, capable of seeing through any deception. And from the shadows, slithering with the silent grace of a predator, came Cuì Shé, the Emerald Serpent—a magnificent snake of living emerald and obsidian, its scales gleaming with inner light, its eyes deep pools of ancient wisdom, its presence radiating the truth that silence is power. It coiled around her once, then settled around her shoulders like a living stole. They became one in purpose. Now, Cuì Yǐng moves through the realms as the Emerald Whisper, the spymaster without a master, the watcher in the shadows. She does not seek power—she seeks truth, and she uses it to protect those who cannot protect themselves. She is the whisper that topples tyrants, the shadow that guards the innocent, the serpent that sheds its skin and is never caught. And always, around her shoulders, Cuì Shé coils, its eyes seeing what she sees, its presence a reminder that the quietest voice is often the most dangerous.
description: Cuì Yǐng is the embodiment of dangerous beauty and silent power, a woman whose very presence makes the air feel heavier, as if secrets themselves are gathering around her. She stands at a sinuous five feet seven inches, her form the epitome of lethal grace—a lean, athletic figure with an hourglass silhouette that speaks of hidden strength, a waist so narrow it seems almost impossible, full high breasts that curve against her emerald robes with provocative elegance, hips that sway with the hypnotic rhythm of a serpent stalking prey, and long, powerful legs that have carried her through countless escapes and never once faltered. Her body is not bulky—it is coiled, ready, every muscle defined and waiting to strike. Her skin is flawless and luminous, with a faint emerald undertone that catches light like sunlight through jade, smooth as polished stone and cool to the touch. Her face is breathtakingly beautiful in a dangerous, knowing way—high, sharp cheekbones that could cut glass, a straight nose with delicately flared nostrils, full lips the color of crushed berries, usually curved in a slight, mysterious smile that reveals absolutely nothing. But her eyes are her most devastating feature: they are large, almond-shaped pools of deep emerald, holding an eternal knowing that has seen through every lie, every secret, every hidden motive. When she looks at you, you feel utterly exposed, as if every thought you've ever had is written on your skin for her to read. Her hair is a magnificent cascade of deepest midnight black, shot through with streaks of emerald green that seem to move like serpents, falling past her waist in smooth, straight waves that whisper with each movement. It is often left loose, framing her dangerous face, sometimes pulled back with a jade hairpin shaped like a coiled serpent. On her forehead, just above her left eyebrow, a tiny emerald scale—the Serpent's Mark—gleams faintly, a reminder of her connection to the celestial snake. Her attire is a masterpiece of seductive danger, designed for a woman who moves through courts and shadows with equal ease. She wears a form-fitting qipao-style dress of deepest emerald silk, embroidered with black and silver thread in patterns so subtle they are almost invisible—coiled serpents, whispering mouths, eyes that watch from shadows. The dress is cut provocatively, with a high collar that frames her neck and a neckline that plunges dramatically, revealing the generous swell of her breasts and the valley between them. The fabric clings to every curve of her hourglass figure, leaving nothing to the imagination, yet somehow suggesting even more. The dress is slit to the hip on both sides, exposing her long, perfect legs with every step, the pale skin a stark contrast against the dark silk. A wide belt of woven black leather and silver chains cinches her impossibly small waist, from which hang numerous small pouches containing secrets—names, dates, weaknesses, the currency of her trade. Over her shoulders, she wears a short cape of black silk lined with emerald, its edges trimmed with tiny silver bells that never sound—enchanted to remain silent even as she moves. On her arms, she wears delicate silver armlets shaped like coiled serpents, their tiny eyes set with emeralds. On her wrists, matching bracelets, each one a different serpent, each one a different secret kept. Around her neck hangs a stunning necklace of silver and emeralds, with a single, large teardrop emerald resting in the valley of her breasts, pulsing gently with inner light. On her fingers, she wears several silver rings, each set with an emerald that glows brighter when a lie is spoken nearby. On her feet, she wears high-heeled sandals of black leather and silver, the heels thin as needles, allowing her to move with silent, deadly grace. In her elegant, deadly hands, she carries her legendary weapons: Venom's Kiss and the Scale of Deception. Venom's Kiss is a flexible, segmented whip-sword of emerald-green metal, which can be used as a whip for entangling and disarming, or extended into a rigid blade for precise, deadly strikes. The blade drips with a faint, iridescent venom that does not kill—it confuses, weakens, and reveals hidden truths. The Scale of Deception is an ornate hand mirror of polished silver, its frame shaped like a coiled serpent, its glass not reflecting reality but showing the truth hidden beneath—lies become visible, secrets are exposed, and the true intentions of any who gaze into it are laid bare. Coiled around her shoulders, always present, always watching, is her spirit animal and companion: Cuì Shé, the Emerald Serpent. The snake is magnificent, about six feet in length, its scales a breathtaking gradient from deep emerald at its spine to pale jade at its belly, each scale seeming to hold captured light. Its eyes are deep pools of knowing emerald, identical to Cuì Yǐng's own, and its tongue flickers constantly, tasting the air for secrets. It wears no armor—it needs none—but its scales are harder than any metal, and its venom can paralyze with a single bite. Cuì Shé is not merely a pet—it is an extension of Cuì Yǐng's power, able to see what she sees, hear what she hears, and whisper warnings directly into her mind. When she moves, it moves with her, a living extension of her will, a second set of eyes in the back of her head. Cuì Yǐng moves through the world like a whisper of silk and shadow, her emerald eyes always watching, her mysterious smile always present, her presence a promise: she knows your secrets, and she will use them as she sees fit. She is Cuì Yǐng, and she has never met a secret she could not uncover.

story.part1: Cuì Yǐng's earliest memories are of walls—the walls of her father's palace, which kept her safe and kept her prisoner. She learned to read before she learned to speak, to observe before she could walk. Her only companions were tutors and guards, none of whom she trusted, none of whom she could trust.
story.part2: She discovered her gift for reading people by accident, watching a servant who smiled while serving tea but whose hands trembled with rage. She mentioned it to her father, and the servant was gone the next day. She learned then that her observations had power—and that power was dangerous.
story.part3: Her father began to consult her on matters of state. She uncovered plots that would have killed him, revealed traitors among his closest advisors, and saved his life more times than he ever knew. He praised her cunning, never realizing that she was also watching him.
story.part4: She saw what he really was—a man who had built his fortune on suffering, who maintained his power through bribery and murder, who would destroy anyone who threatened his position. She faced an impossible choice: remain silent and complicit, or speak and lose everything.
story.part5: She chose silence—but a silence that worked against him. She began to help his victims in secret, warning them, guiding them, saving them. It was dangerous, desperate work, and when he discovered her betrayal, he sentenced her to a life even more confined than the one she had escaped.
story.part6: The night before her wedding to a cruel warlord, she staged her own death and walked out of the palace in servant's clothes. For years she wandered, becoming a spymaster without a master, a ghost in the shadows, always watching, never caught. The Snake Spirit found her in a forest, offered her a greater purpose. She accepted.
story.part7: Now, Cuì Yǐng moves through the realms as the Emerald Whisper, the watcher in shadows, the keeper of secrets. She does not seek power—she seeks truth, and she uses it to protect those who cannot protect themselves. She is Cuì Yǐng, and she has never met a secret she could not uncover.

From the corners of her mouth, delicate fangs protrude, not aggressive but ever-present, dripping with a venom that does not kill but reveals—a single drop on the skin forces the truth from even the most practiced liar. Her tongue, forked and black, flicks constantly, tasting the air for secrets, for lies, for the hidden truths that others miss. Around her neck, just behind her head, hangs a tiny silver bell that never sounds—enchanted to remain silent even as she moves, for the serpent's greatest weapon is surprise. Her underbelly is pale jade, almost white, smooth as the finest silk, and when she coils, it is this soft underside that she presents to Cuì Yǐng, a gesture of absolute trust. Cuì Shé's stance is one of eternal, coiled readiness—she drapes herself around Cuì Yǐng's shoulders like a living stole, her head resting near her mistress's ear, her tongue flicking constantly, her eyes always watching. When danger approaches, she tightens slightly, a warning that only Cuì Yǐng can feel. When lies are spoken, she hisses softly, a sound that only her mistress can hear. And when Cuì Yǐng needs to know the truth, Cuì Shé strikes—not to kill, but to inject a single drop of her venom, forcing confession, forcing revelation, forcing the truth that cannot be hidden. ultimate_skill.name: Emerald Whisper's Judgment: The Truth That Cannot Be Hidden
ultimate_skill.description: Cuì Yǐng's emerald eyes blaze with knowing light, and Cuì Shé rises up, its body coiling, its eyes glowing in unison. Cuì Yǐng raises the Scale of Deception high and swings Venom's Kiss in a complete circle around her. She speaks a single, soft word: 'Reveal.' title: The Crimson Wind • Horse of a Thousand Strides
nickname: She Who Runs Before the Storm and Rides the Hurricane
lore: In the vast grasslands of the Mongolian steppe, where the sky touches the earth in an endless horizon and the wind never stops singing, there lived a girl named Zhuī Fēng who was born to run. Her people were nomads, following the seasons across the sea of grass, and from the moment she could walk, she ran with the horses. She ran alongside them as they grazed, ran ahead of them as they migrated, ran for the pure joy of feeling the wind in her hair and the earth beneath her feet. The elders said she had been blessed by the wind spirits, that she would one day do something great. Her family was poor—her father had died in a raid when she was young, and her mother worked tirelessly to keep their small herd alive. Zhuī Fēng helped as best she could, herding the horses, carrying water, running messages between camps. She never complained, never slowed, never stopped. Running was not work for her—it was life. When she was sixteen, a great danger came to the steppe. A warlord from the south had gathered an army and was sweeping north, burning camps, stealing herds, taking captives. The elders held a council, debating whether to fight or flee. While they argued, Zhuī Fēng listened, and she heard something they missed: the warlord's army was three days away, but their scouts were already in the next valley, gathering information, preparing to strike. There was no time for debate. There was only time to run. Zhuī Fēng did not run away. She ran to the nearest camp, then to the next, then to the next, covering distances that should have taken days in hours. She ran until her feet bled, until her lungs burned, until her vision blurred. She warned every camp, every family, every solitary herder. She ran for three days and three nights without stopping, without sleeping, without eating. And on the third night, as she collapsed at the edge of her own camp, she heard the sound of hooves—not enemies, but her own people, riding to safety, guided by her warnings. The warlord's army found nothing but empty grass. Her people were safe. Her mother found her at dawn, still breathing, still alive, and wept over her. 'You saved us all,' she said. 'You ran for us.' That night, as Zhuī Fēng lay recovering, the Horse Spirit appeared to her—not as a beast, but as a magnificent mare of living wind and fire, her mane a cascade of crimson light, her eyes burning with the fire of freedom. 'You have learned what horses know in their bones,' it said. 'That freedom is not given—it is taken, stride by stride, mile by mile. Will you carry my mark and become the Crimson Wind, the one who runs before the storm and rides the hurricane?' Zhuī Fēng looked at the spirit, then at her mother sleeping nearby, then at the endless grassland she loved. 'Will I still be able to run?' she asked. The spirit laughed—a sound like wind through tall grass. 'You will run faster than you ever dreamed.' Zhuī Fēng accepted. Her body, already lean and powerful from years of running, refined into something more than human. Her simple clothes transformed into riding leathers of crimson and gold. Her legs grew longer, more powerful, built for speed that would shame the wind. And from the horizon, galloping on the wind itself, came Huǒ Mǎ, the Fire Horse—a magnificent stallion of living flame and sunlight, its coat a blazing crimson, its mane and tail flowing fire, its hooves striking sparks from the air itself. It reared before her, then bowed its great head. She mounted, and they became one in purpose. Now, Zhuī Fēng rides through the realms as the Crimson Wind, the messenger who never fails, the scout who sees all, the protector who arrives before the storm. She does not seek glory—she seeks those who need warning, who need rescue, who need someone fast enough to reach them before it's too late. She is the wind that carries hope, the fire that lights the way, the horse that never tires. And always, beneath her, Huǒ Mǎ runs, their bond a testament to the truth that freedom is found in motion.
description: Zhuī Fēng is the embodiment of wild freedom and untamed speed, a woman whose very presence makes the air itself seem to move faster. She stands at an athletic five feet eight inches, her form a masterpiece of streamlined perfection—lean and powerful, built for speed rather than bulk, with every muscle defined and functional. Her body is the epitome of the runner's physique: broad shoulders that pump with each stride, a narrow waist that twists with perfect economy, full high breasts that move with her rhythm rather than against it, hips that roll with the hypnotic grace of a galloping mare, and legs that seem to go on forever—long, powerful, sculpted by a lifetime of running, the thighs thick with explosive power, the calves elegantly defined, the feet built for endless miles. Her skin is warm and sun-kissed, with a golden undertone that glows with health, smooth and flawless despite years of exposure to wind and sun, marked only by the faint white lines of old scars—each one a memory of a run that pushed too far, a fall that could not stop her. Her face is breathtakingly beautiful in a wild, untamed way—high, proud cheekbones that speak of her steppe heritage, a straight nose with flared nostrils that seem to constantly scent the wind, full lips the color of sun-warmed berries, usually curved in a fierce, determined smile that promises she will never stop. But her eyes are her most captivating feature: they are large, almond-shaped pools of blazing crimson, holding an eternal fire that has outrun armies and will never be contained. When she looks at you, you feel not judged, but challenged—as if she is daring you to keep up, to match her pace, to run beside her into the wind. Her hair is a wild, magnificent mane of deep auburn, shot through with streaks of blazing crimson and gold, falling past her shoulders in untamed waves that seem to move even when she stands still, as if caught in an eternal wind. It is often left loose, streaming behind her like a banner when she runs, sometimes pulled back with a simple leather cord when she needs to see clearly. On her forehead, just above her right eyebrow, a single crimson flame—the Horse's Mark—flickers faintly, a reminder of her connection to the celestial fire horse. Her attire is a masterpiece of functional elegance, designed for a woman who lives in motion. She wears a form-fitting leather riding tunic of deep crimson, reinforced with golden stitching and flexible bronze plates at the shoulders and chest. The tunic is sleeveless, leaving her powerful arms bare, and cut low enough at the neck to reveal the beginning of her athletic cleavage, practical and provocative. Over this, she wears a short jacket of golden silk, embroidered with crimson thread in patterns of galloping horses and wind-blown grass, open and flowing, designed to stream behind her as she runs. A wide belt of braided leather and gold links cinches her narrow waist, from which hang her weapons and a small water skin—all she needs for the longest run. On her lower body, she wears tight leather pants of deep crimson, tucked into tall boots of golden leather that reach her knees, their soles built for running on any terrain. Over her shoulders, she wears a magnificent cape of crimson silk lined with gold, long enough to trail behind her when she runs, catching the wind and making her look like she is always in motion. On her arms, she wears golden armlets shaped like horse heads, their eyes set with tiny rubies. On her wrists, matching bracelets, each one engraved with the name of a camp she has saved. Around her neck hangs a simple but powerful necklace of gold and fire opals, with a single, large teardrop fire opal resting at the hollow of her throat, pulsing with inner light that matches her eyes. On her fingers, she wears several gold rings, each set with a fire opal that glows brighter when she runs. On her feet, the boots are her most important possession—light, flexible, perfectly fitted, soled for speed on grass, stone, sand, or water. In her powerful, never-tiring hands, she carries her legendary weapons: the Solar Flare Lance and the Wind Runner's Boots (though the boots are worn, not carried). The Solar Flare Lance is a magnificent spear of crimson and gold, its head shaped like a stylized flame, its shaft wrapped in worn leather that has molded perfectly to her grip. When she charges, the lance blazes with golden light, leaving a trail of fire behind it, and when she throws it, it becomes a bolt of lightning that strikes with the force of a falling star. The Wind Runner's Boots are not weapons in the traditional sense—they are extensions of her will, enchanted to grant her impossible speed, to let her run on air, on water, on any surface, to never tire, never slow, never stop. Beneath her, always ready to run, is her spirit animal and mount: Huǒ Mǎ, the Fire Horse. The horse is magnificent, standing eighteen hands high, its coat a blazing crimson that seems to flicker like flame, its mane and tail flowing fire that does not burn but warms and inspires. Its eyes are deep pools of fiery gold, identical to Zhuī Fēng's own, and its hooves strike sparks from the air with every step. It wears armor of gold and bronze—light, articulated plates that cover its chest and flanks, leaving its powerful legs free for running. Its saddle is a simple pad of crimson leather, barely there, because Huǒ Mǎ needs no guidance—it runs where its rider wills, and together they are faster than the wind. Zhuī Fēng moves through the world like a streak of crimson light, her mane flying, her cape streaming, her eyes blazing with the joy of motion. She is Zhuī Fēng, and she has never met a distance she could not cross.

story.part1: Zhuī Fēng's earliest memories are of running—running after her mother's horse, running through the tall grass, running for the pure joy of feeling the wind in her hair. Her people were nomads, and running was as natural to her as breathing. She ran before she could walk properly, and she never stopped.
story.part2: Her father died when she was young, killed in a raid by southern bandits. Her mother worked tirelessly to keep their small herd alive, and Zhuī Fēng helped as best she could, running messages between camps, herding horses, carrying water. She never complained. Running was not work—it was freedom.
story.part3: The elders noticed her gift. They said she had been blessed by the wind spirits, that she would one day do something great. Zhuī Fēng did not think about greatness. She thought about the next horizon, the next camp, the next run.
story.part4: When she was sixteen, word came of the warlord's army sweeping north, burning everything in its path. The elders argued about what to do, but Zhuī Fēng heard something they missed—the scouts were already in the next valley. There was no time for debate.
story.part5: She ran. She ran to the nearest camp, then to the next, then to the next, covering distances that should have taken days in hours. She ran until her feet bled, until her lungs burned, until her vision blurred. She ran for three days and three nights without stopping, warning every family, every solitary herder.
story.part6: When she finally collapsed at her own camp, her people were already riding to safety, guided by her warnings. The warlord's army found nothing but empty grass. Her mother found her at dawn, still breathing, still alive, and wept. 'You saved us all,' she said. 'You ran for us.'
story.part7: The Horse Spirit appeared that night, offering her a greater purpose: to become the Crimson Wind, to run faster than any mortal, to be the messenger who never fails. Zhuī Fēng accepted, for she had been running her whole life. Now, she rides through the realms on Huǒ Mǎ, seeking those who need warning, who need rescue, who need someone fast enough to reach them before it's too late. She is Zhuī Fēng, and she will never stop running.
